x-m-e1-01.title: Showing 52 in different ways with bundles and single ones
x-m-e1-01.goal: Use the fact that trading 1 bundle of 10 for 10 single ones keeps the total the same, show the same number with different bundles and single ones, and find and fix a wrong solution.
x-m-e1-01.material: Harin solved a marble story like this. There are 3 bundles of 10 marbles and 12 single marbles. You want to find out how many there are in all.
x-m-e1-01.thinking.0: Finding the part that was left out in a solution
x-m-e1-01.thinking.1: Showing the same number in different ways
x-m-e1-01.thinking.2: Checking by yourself whether the way you showed it is right
x-m-e1-01.prereq.0: Counting and reading numbers with bundles of 10 and single ones (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick the wrong line in Harin's solution.
x-m-e1-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check one by one how each line follows from the line right before it.
x-m-e1-01.s.s1.hint.1: If you made a new bundle from single ones, count how many bundles there are in all after that.
x-m-e1-01.s.s1.line.0: There are 3 bundles of 10 marbles and 12 single marbles.
x-m-e1-01.s.s1.line.2: If you make bundles of 10 from the 12 single ones, you get 1 bundle and 2 single ones.
x-m-e1-01.s.s1.line.3: So that is 3 bundles and 2 single ones, 32 marbles in all.
x-m-e1-01.s.s1.explain: The 4th line is wrong. In the 3rd line, a new bundle was made from 12 single ones, but in the 4th line this bundle was not counted and the bundles were left at 3. The bundles are 3 and 1 together, which is 4, and there are 2 single ones, so it is 42. If you add 30 and 12 right away, it is also 42. Lines 1 to 3 are right.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.prompt: You want to show 52 marbles as a bundles of 10 and b single ones. Make 3 different ways.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.hint.0: Pick the number of bundles, and count how many single ones you need to make 52.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how many single ones you get when you undo one bundle, and change the answer you made before.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The bundles and single ones are counts of 0 or more.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please write the bundles and single ones as counts like 0, 1, 2, 3...
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The total is 52, which is right.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The total number of marbles is not 52. Count each bundle as 10 and each single one as 1.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.explain: 5 bundles and 2 single ones, 4 bundles and 12 single ones, 3 bundles and 22 single ones, 2 bundles and 32 single ones. Each time there is one less bundle, there are 10 more single ones, and it is 52 in all.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Write how many more single ones there are when there is one less bundle, and say why it is still 52 in all.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put the number of bundles and single ones of the two ways you just made side by side and compare them.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Think about what changes and what stays the same when you undo 1 bundle and turn it into single ones.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: When there are fewer bundles...
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is it clear in your explanation how many single ones 1 bundle equals?
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write that the total stays the same because you get as many single ones as the bundles you lost?
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.because.model.0: When there is 1 less bundle, there are 10 more single ones. 1 bundle equals 10 single ones, so it is still 52 in all.
x-m-e1-01.s.s2.because.model.1: If you undo one bundle, you get 10 single ones. So only the shape changes, and the number stays the same.

x-m-e1-02.title: Finding the secret number: do we need more clues?
x-m-e1-02.goal: Find for yourself that there are several numbers that meet all the given clues, and decide what more clues are needed to pin down the secret number to one.
x-m-e1-02.material: Hajun picked a secret number. Clue 1: It is a number greater than 50 and less than 70. Clue 2: The number of single ones is greater than the number of bundles of 10. (Example: 34 is 3 bundles and 4 single ones, and 4 is greater than 3, so it fits clue 2.)
x-m-e1-02.thinking.0: Finding numbers that meet all the conditions
x-m-e1-02.thinking.1: Judging whether there is enough information
x-m-e1-02.thinking.2: Comparing how much a new clue narrows down the candidates
x-m-e1-02.prereq.0: Reading and writing numbers up to 100, comparing two numbers (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.prompt: Find 3 different numbers that fit both clue 1 and clue 2, and write each as a bundles of 10 and b single ones.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.hint.0: First think of the numbers that can be the number of bundles, then decide the single ones.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether the number you picked is greater than 50 and less than 70, and whether the single ones are more than the bundles.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.ok.c1: The bundles and single ones are in the right form.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.fail.c1: Please write the number of bundles as 0 or more and the single ones as a number from 0 to 9.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.ok.c2: It is a number greater than 50 and less than 70.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.fail.c2: That number is not greater than 50 and less than 70.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.ok.c3: The number of single ones is greater than the number of bundles.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.fail.c3: The number of single ones is not greater than the number of bundles of 10.
x-m-e1-02.s.s1.explain: The numbers that fit are 56, 57, 58, 59, 67, 68, and 69, 7 in all. Two clues alone cannot pin it down to one.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.prompt: Hajun wants to give one more clue. Choose all the clues that, used together with clues 1 and 2, let you pin down the secret number to exactly one.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write all the numbers that fit clues 1 and 2.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.hint.1: Apply each clue in the options one by one and count how many numbers are left.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.r.a: Both 58 and 68 are left, so it is not pinned down to one.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.o.b: It is greater than 60 and the single ones are 7.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.r.b: The candidates greater than 60 are 67, 68, and 69, and only one of them has 7 single ones.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.o.c: It has 6 bundles and fewer than 9 single ones.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.r.c: 67 and 68 are left, so it is not pinned down to one.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.o.d: It is a number greater than 58 and less than 60.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.r.d: Only one of the candidates falls in this range.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.o.e: It is a number less than 70.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.r.e: This is already in clue 1, so the candidates do not get fewer.
x-m-e1-02.s.s2.explain: The candidates are 56, 57, 58, 59, 67, 68, and 69. You can find out by adding one clue and counting how many candidates are left. If the single ones are 8, then 58 and 68 are left; if it has 6 bundles and fewer than 9 single ones, then 67 and 68 are left. If it is greater than 60 and the single ones are 7, only 67 is left, and if it is greater than 58 and less than 60, only 59 is left.

x-m-e1-03.title: "It got fewer, so I should subtract" - is that right?
x-m-e1-03.goal: Learn that you should not choose the equation just from the word "got fewer," and that you choose it by thinking about whether what you want to find is the number before it got fewer or after.
x-m-e1-03.material: Doyun is solving this problem: "There were some marbles. I gave 4 to a friend and then 6 were left. How many marbles were there at first?"
x-m-e1-03.thinking.0: Finding the wrong reason in a solution
x-m-e1-03.thinking.1: Checking backward whether the answer fits the story
x-m-e1-03.prereq.0: Experience with adding and subtracting numbers within 20 (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-03.s.s1.prompt: Pick the wrong line in Doyun's solution. (You can pick just one line.)
x-m-e1-03.s.s1.hint.0: First think about which is more, the marbles at first or the marbles left.
x-m-e1-03.s.s1.hint.1: Take Doyun's answer of 2 marbles and act out the story: if you give away 4, are 6 really left?
x-m-e1-03.s.s1.line.0: There were some marbles, and when I gave away 4, 6 were left.
x-m-e1-03.s.s1.line.1: I gave some away, so the marbles got fewer. So I subtract.
x-m-e1-03.s.s1.explain: Lines 2 and 3 are wrong. It is true that the marbles got fewer, but this problem asks for the number before it got fewer, that is, the number at first, not the number after it got fewer. At first there must have been more than the 6 that were left. If you give away 4 from the answer of 2 in line 3, you cannot have 6 left, so it does not fit the story.
x-m-e1-03.s.s2.prompt: Which equation correctly finds the number of marbles at first?
x-m-e1-03.s.s2.hint.0: Try the story backward. If the friend gives back the 4, how many marbles will there be?
x-m-e1-03.s.s2.hint.1: Act out the story again with the answer of each equation and check whether the number left is 6.
x-m-e1-03.s.s2.r.a: This is Doyun's equation. The answer to this equation does not fit the story.
x-m-e1-03.s.s2.r.b: This equation treats 10 as if you already know it is the number at first. The number at first is a number you don't know yet.
x-m-e1-03.s.s2.r.c: This equation sees the number left and the number given away coming together to make the number before it got fewer.
x-m-e1-03.s.s2.r.d: You added the 4 marbles given away two times. The 4 were given away only once.
x-m-e1-03.s.s2.explain: If you put together the 6 left and the 4 given to the friend, you get the number of marbles before it got fewer. If you give away 4 from 10, 6 are left.
x-m-e1-03.s.s3.prompt: This time, make stories. There were x marbles, and when I gave away y, 6 were left. Make 3 with different numbers of marbles at first. (At most 20 marbles at first, and at least 1 given away)
x-m-e1-03.s.s3.hint.0: Pick the number of marbles given away, and think about how many marbles there must have been at first for 6 to be left.
x-m-e1-03.s.s3.hint.1: Read your story out loud and check that 6 are really left.
x-m-e1-03.s.s3.ok.c1: The numbers are in the right range.
x-m-e1-03.s.s3.fail.c1: Please write the marbles at first as 20 or fewer, and the marbles given away as a count of 1 or more like 1, 2, 3...
x-m-e1-03.s.s3.fail.c2: The marbles left after giving away are not 6. Take away the marbles given from the marbles at first.
x-m-e1-03.s.s3.explain: If there were 8 at first, give 2; if 10, give 4; if 15, give 9, and 6 are left. The more marbles given away, the more marbles there must have been at first.

x-m-e1-04.title: People got off and on the bus, but the number of people stayed the same
x-m-e1-04.goal: Learn what must happen for the total to stay the same when something decreases and something increases together, and make such cases yourself.
x-m-e1-04.material: There were 10 people on a bus. At one stop, some people got off and some people got on. Then there were still 10 people on the bus.
x-m-e1-04.thinking.0: Figuring out the changes in a story (getting fewer and getting more)
x-m-e1-04.thinking.1: Making several cases that fit the conditions
x-m-e1-04.prereq.0: Experience with stories where numbers around 10 get more or fewer (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.prompt: What can you tell from this story?
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think separately about what makes the number of people on the bus go down and what makes it go up.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.hint.1: For example, if 2 people get off and 5 get on, think about whether there will be more or fewer than 10 people on the bus.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.o.a: More people got off than got on.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.r.a: If more people got off, the number of people on the bus goes below 10.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.o.b: More people got on than got off.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.r.b: If more people got on, the number of people on the bus goes above 10.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.o.c: The number of people who got off and the number of people who got on are the same.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.r.c: I thought that it went down by some, then went up by the same amount, so it became the same as at first.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.r.d: The story says some people got on. If nobody got on, it does not match the story.
x-m-e1-04.s.s1.explain: It goes down by the number who got off and up by the number who got on. If it is still 10, the number who got off and the number who got on must be the same.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different cases that fit the story. Write the number who got off, a, and the number who got on, b. (Both are at least 1, and the number who got off is at most 10.)
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.hint.0: Decide the number who got off first, and count how many people are on the bus.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.hint.1: Then decide the number who got on and check that it is 10 again.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of people are right.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please write the people who got off and the people who got on as at least 1, and the people who got off as at most 10.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.ok.c2: There are still 10 people on the bus.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The number of people on the bus did not stay at 10. Count the number that went down and the number that went up again.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.explain: If the two numbers are the same, like 2 getting off and 2 getting on, or 5 getting off and 5 getting on, it stays at 10.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.because.prompt: Say why the number of people on the bus stays the same when the number who got off and the number who got on are the same.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Say separately what happens on the bus because of the people who got off and what happens because of the people who got on.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Pick one number (for example, 3 people) and follow the story.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation have both what makes it go down and what makes it go up?
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say that the number that went down and the number that went up are the same?
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.because.model.0: 3 people got off, so it went down by 3, but 3 people got on, so it went up again, so it stays the same.
x-m-e1-04.s.s2.because.model.1: As many new people get on as got off and sit in the seats, so the seats are filled again. As many come in as left, so it is the same.

x-m-e1-05.title: Checking the claim "If it rolls, it is a ball shape"
x-m-e1-05.goal: Check whether the claim "Everything that rolls is a ball shape" is right using the features of several objects, and fix the claim so it is right.
x-m-e1-05.material: Seojun said, "Everything that rolls is a ball shape. A marble rolls and a soccer ball rolls!" In the room there are a marble, a soccer ball, a snack box (box shape), and a drink can (cylinder shape). (The can has a flat, round top and bottom, and the side is curved all the way around.)
x-m-e1-05.thinking.1: Choosing an object that is a counterexample
x-m-e1-05.prereq.0: Recognizing and naming box shapes, cylinder shapes, and ball shapes (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-05.s.s1.prompt: What is a way to show that Seojun's claim is wrong?
x-m-e1-05.s.s1.explain: To show that Seojun's claim is wrong, you only need one object that rolls but is not a ball shape. The can is a cylinder shape, and it rolls if you lay it on its side and push it.
x-m-e1-05.s.s2.prompt: What would you like to tell Seojun? Use an example object to fix Seojun's claim and write it correctly.
x-m-e1-05.s.s2.hint.0: First write the name and shape of the object you just picked.
x-m-e1-05.s.s2.hint.1: Also write how you make that object roll.
x-m-e1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is it clear that the object you gave is not a ball shape?
x-m-e1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that ball shapes are not the only shapes that roll?
x-m-e1-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about how to place it so it rolls?
x-m-e1-05.s.s2.model.0: No. A drink can is a cylinder shape, but if you lay it down and roll it, it rolls. Not only ball shapes roll.
x-m-e1-05.s.s2.model.1: Not just a marble, a can rolls too if you lay it down. So not everything that rolls is a ball shape.

x-m-e1-06.title: What shape is the object in the box?
x-m-e1-06.goal: Each time you get one more clue, narrow down the possible shapes and fix your first idea to fit the new clue.
x-m-e1-06.material: You are blindfolded and feel an object in a box, and you hear clues one at a time. The object in the box is one of a box shape, a cylinder shape, or a ball shape.
x-m-e1-06.thinking.0: Narrowing down the possible shapes with clues
x-m-e1-06.thinking.1: Fixing your idea with new clues
x-m-e1-06.thinking.2: Comparing which clue sorts out the shapes best
x-m-e1-06.prereq.0: Knowing the features of box shapes, cylinder shapes, and ball shapes (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.prompt: The clues are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your idea.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write down box shape, cylinder shape, and ball shape, and for each clue mark the shapes that are possible.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think one by one about which shapes each clue rules out.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Clue 1: When I pushed it with my hand, it rolled and rolled.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.after: If it rolls, it is unlikely to be a box shape. Ball shape and cylinder shape are left.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Only a ball shape is possible.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: A cylinder shape also rolls if you lay it on its side and push it. You decided on one possibility too fast.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It could be a box shape.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: A box shape has many flat faces, so when you push it, it slides and has a hard time rolling.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It could be a ball shape or a cylinder shape.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought of all the shapes that roll.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: You can't tell anything from one clue.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You can make a box shape less likely. The clue is not useless.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.1.info: Clue 2: I put the object on the floor and put a book on top of it, and the book did not fall off and stayed still.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.1.after: For a book to stay on top, the top must be flat. A ball shape has no flat part. A cylinder shape became more likely.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: You still can't tell a ball shape and a cylinder shape apart.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You didn't use the new clue that the book stays still. On a ball, a book easily rolls off.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Clue 1 said it rolled, so it doesn't fit a box shape well.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: A cylinder shape is more likely.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You used the new clue to pick a shape with a flat top. You fixed your idea.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.2.info: Clue 3: I felt the face where the book was, and it is a flat, round shape.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: Choose what could be the object in the box.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.2.after: If it has a flat, round face, it is a cylinder shape. A drink can and a tuna can both fit.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: A marble is a ball shape, so it has no flat face.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It is a cylinder shape with a flat, round top.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: A die is a box shape, so its faces are squares.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: It is a cylinder shape with a flat, round top.
x-m-e1-06.s.s1.reflect: How were the possible shapes different when you knew only clue 1 and when you knew up to clue 2? If you first thought "only a ball shape," which clue made you change your mind?

x-m-e1-07.title: Length measured with paper clips and glue sticks: which one is longer?
x-m-e1-07.goal: Learn that lengths measured with different units cannot be compared by counts alone, and decide what information you need to compare them.
x-m-e1-07.material: Minjun measured the length of a pencil with paper clips and got 5 paper clips. Seoyun measured the length of a colored pencil with glue sticks (stick-shaped glue) and got 3 glue sticks. Both laid them in one line side by side with no gaps. Which is longer, the pencil or the colored pencil?
x-m-e1-07.thinking.0: Picking out the information needed for comparing
x-m-e1-07.thinking.1: Making cases that fit the conditions
x-m-e1-07.thinking.2: Fixing a claim that was judged only by counts
x-m-e1-07.prereq.0: Measuring the length of things by the number of the same unit (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.prompt: What information would let you know which one is longer? Choose all that fit.
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.hint.0: Is one paper clip the same length as one glue stick? Think about it first.
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what must be the same to compare two lengths, and find in the options the information that lets you know that.
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.r.a: The order of measuring has nothing to do with length.
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.o.b: How many paper clips 1 glue stick is
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.r.b: This is information that lets you change glue sticks and paper clips into the same unit.
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.r.c: Thickness has nothing to do with length.
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.o.d: The result of putting the two objects side by side with one end lined up and comparing them
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.r.d: This is a way to compare directly without using different units.
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.o.e: The result of counting again how many times you put the paper clips and the glue sticks
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.r.e: Even if the counts are right, if the units are different, you cannot compare the lengths by counts alone.
x-m-e1-07.s.s1.explain: A paper clip and a glue stick are different lengths, so you cannot compare by looking at just 5 and 3. If you know how many paper clips 1 glue stick is, you can compare in the same unit, and you can also compare the pencil and the colored pencil directly by lining up one end.
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.prompt: Say that the length of 1 glue stick is p paper clips. For the colored pencil (3 glue sticks) to be longer than the pencil (5 paper clips), what could p be? Find 2 different values of p. (p is a whole number from 1 to 6.)
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.hint.0: When p is 1, find how many paper clips 3 glue sticks is and compare with 5.
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.hint.1: Change p to 1, 2, 3 and write in a table how many paper clips 3 glue sticks is.
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.var.p: How many paper clips 1 glue stick is
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.ok.c1: p is a whole number from 1 to 6.
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.fail.c1: Please write p as a whole number from 1 to 6.
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.ok.c2: 3 glue sticks are longer than 5 paper clips.
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.fail.c2: 3 glue sticks are not longer than 5 paper clips. Count how many paper clips 3 glue sticks equal.
x-m-e1-07.s.s2.explain: If p is 2, 3 glue sticks are 6 paper clips, which is longer than 5. If p is 1, it is 3 paper clips, so the pencil is longer. The result changes depending on the length of 1 glue stick.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.prompt: Minjun said, "5 is greater than 3, so my pencil is longer!" What is a right way to think about Minjun's claim?
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.hint.0: With the values of p you found earlier, find the cases where Minjun's claim is right and the cases where it is wrong.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about what must be the same for the side with the bigger count to always be longer.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.o.a: That's right. The side with the bigger count is longer.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.r.a: Only when the unit is the same is the side with more longer. Remember what happened earlier when p was 2.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.o.b: No. The side measured with glue sticks is always longer.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.r.b: If 1 glue stick equals 1 paper clip, 3 glue sticks are 3 paper clips, so it is shorter.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.o.c: The units are different, so you need to know the length of 1.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.r.c: You thought about the fact that with different units you can't compare by counts alone.
x-m-e1-07.s.s3.explain: A paper clip and a glue stick are different lengths, so you can't compare by counts alone. Depending on how many paper clips 1 glue stick is, the pencil may be longer or the colored pencil may be longer.

x-m-e1-08.title: If the long hand is on 6, is it "6 minutes"?
x-m-e1-08.goal: Learn that the short hand and the long hand on a clock tell different things, and find and fix the wrong part in Minseo's reading of the time.
x-m-e1-08.material: Minseo read a clock. The short hand of the clock is between 7 and 8, and the long hand points to 6. (There is no picture of the clock. On the clock face, 12 is at the very top and 6 is at the very bottom.)
x-m-e1-08.thinking.0: Finding the wrong reason in a solution
x-m-e1-08.thinking.2: Explaining how to read a clock
x-m-e1-08.prereq.0: Telling the short hand and long hand of a clock apart, reading o'clock times (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-08.s.s1.prompt: Pick the wrong line in how Minseo read the time. (You can pick just one line.)
x-m-e1-08.s.s1.hint.0: Remember how you read it when the long hand points to 12.
x-m-e1-08.s.s1.line.0: The short hand is between 7 and 8, so 7 o'clock has passed.
x-m-e1-08.s.s1.line.1: The long hand points to 6, so it is 6 minutes.
x-m-e1-08.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. When the long hand points to 6, you read it as 30 minutes, not 6 minutes. It is when the long hand, which started at 12, has gone half a turn to 6. Line 3 just follows line 2, so it is not right either. Line 1 is right.
x-m-e1-08.s.s2.prompt: Which is the correctly fixed time for what Minseo read?
x-m-e1-08.s.s2.hint.0: Look at which two numbers the short hand is between, and decide which hour has passed.
x-m-e1-08.s.s2.hint.1: Decide how many minutes the place the long hand points to is read as, and then match it with the options.
x-m-e1-08.s.s2.r.c: The short hand has not passed 8 yet.
x-m-e1-08.s.s2.explain: The short hand is between 7 and 8, so 7 o'clock has passed, and the long hand is on 6, so it is 30 minutes. So it is 7:30.
x-m-e1-08.s.s3.prompt: Teach Minseo how to read a clock. Write what the short hand and the long hand each tell.
x-m-e1-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write separately what you read with the short hand and what you read with the long hand.
x-m-e1-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write separately what the short hand and the long hand tell?
x-m-e1-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the reason or the way that long hand 6 is read as 30 minutes?
x-m-e1-08.s.s3.model.0: The short hand tells what hour it is, and when the long hand points to 6, it is 30 minutes. So it is 7:30.
x-m-e1-08.s.s3.model.1: Read the hour with the short hand first, and then read the minutes with the long hand. If the long hand is on 6, it has gone half a turn, so it is 30 minutes.

x-m-e1-09.title: What bead comes next? Guess the pattern and fix it
x-m-e1-09.goal: Learn that with little data a pattern can be read in several ways, and fix your idea about the pattern each time there is more data.
x-m-e1-09.material: Apple-shaped beads and grape-shaped beads are strung on a necklace by some pattern. I will show you the beads one at a time from the left.
x-m-e1-09.thinking.0: Thinking about the possible patterns from little data
x-m-e1-09.thinking.1: Fixing your first idea with new data
x-m-e1-09.thinking.2: Predicting the next one with the pattern
x-m-e1-09.prereq.0: Recognizing shapes or numbers that repeat (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.prompt: The beads are revealed one at a time. Each time, choose your idea.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write the beads you have seen so far in order, and group and mark the part that repeats.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.hint.1: Rebuild the earlier beads with the pattern you thought of and check that it is the same as what you saw.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.info: The first three are apple, grape, apple.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: What will the fourth bead be?
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.after: With only three, both a pattern that alternates and a pattern that repeats every three are possible. You have to see more to decide.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is grape. I think apple and grape come out in turns.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You found the alternating pattern. Think about whether other patterns are possible too.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is apple. I think the three beads apple, grape, apple repeat.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You found the pattern that repeats every three. Think about whether other patterns are possible too.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I can't decide on one. I need to see more.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought about the fact that the pattern is not pinned down to one because there is little data.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: A new strawberry-shaped bead comes out.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: So far there are only apples and grapes. There is no reason to think a new shape will come out.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.1.info: Looking up to five, they are apple, grape, apple, apple, grape.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now what do you think about the pattern?
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.1.after: If the pattern were alternating, the fourth would have to be grape. It fits the pattern that repeats every three better.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If you see apple, grape, apple repeating, there is a pattern.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The alternating pattern is right, and only the fourth one happened to be different.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: If it were alternating, the fourth would have had to be grape. You need to fix your first idea after seeing the new data.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It might be a pattern where the three beads apple, grape, apple repeat.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You fixed your idea to fit the new data.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.2.info: Looking up to nine, they are apple, grape, apple, apple, grape, apple, apple, grape, apple.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: What will the tenth bead be?
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Grapes are at the 2nd, 5th, and 8th places. They skip by three. The next grape is the 11th.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You found the first place of the new start in the pattern that repeats every three.
x-m-e1-09.s.s1.reflect: How did your idea about the pattern change between seeing only three and seeing nine? What got better the more beads you saw?
x-m-e1-09.s.s2.prompt: A friend said, "You can know the pattern by looking at just the first three. You don't need to look at the rest." What is a right way to think about this?
x-m-e1-09.s.s2.hint.0: Remember whether the fourth bead was pinned down to one when you saw only the first three.
x-m-e1-09.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many possible patterns there were and how many were left as the data grew.
x-m-e1-09.s.s2.explain: With only three, both a pattern that alternates and a pattern that repeats every three were possible. As the data grew, it was narrowed down to one. How many you need to see depends on the data.

x-m-e1-10.title: Making a pattern where the fourth number is 12
x-m-e1-10.goal: Make a pattern that keeps growing by the same amount yourself, and find out that even if one number is the same, there can be several patterns.
x-m-e1-10.material: Let's make patterns that line up numbers. Start from the first number and keep growing by the same amount. For example, 1, 3, 5, 7 starts at 1 and grows by 2.
x-m-e1-10.thinking.0: Making a pattern that fits the conditions
x-m-e1-10.thinking.1: Judging whether one piece of information determines the pattern
x-m-e1-10.prereq.0: Counting numbers in order and finding that they grow by the same amount (Grade 1 level)
x-m-e1-10.s.s1.prompt: Make 2 different patterns where the fourth number is 12. a is the first number and d is the amount it grows by. (Both are at least 1.)
x-m-e1-10.s.s1.hint.0: Decide the amount it grows by first, then go backward from 12, taking away that amount each time, to find the first number.
x-m-e1-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write the numbers you made in order and check that the fourth is 12.
x-m-e1-10.s.s1.ok.c1: The first number and the amount it grows by are right.
x-m-e1-10.s.s1.fail.c1: Please write the first number and the amount it grows by as whole numbers of 1 or more.
x-m-e1-10.s.s1.fail.c2: The fourth number is not 12. Start from the first number and add the amount it grows by three times.
x-m-e1-10.s.s1.explain: 6, 8, 10, 12 starts at 6 and grows by 2, 3, 6, 9, 12 starts at 3 and grows by 3, and 9, 10, 11, 12 starts at 9 and grows by 1.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.prompt: If you only know that "the fourth number is 12," is the pattern pinned down to one?
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.hint.0: Find the fifth number for each of the two patterns you made earlier.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the fifth numbers of the two patterns are the same.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.o.a: It is pinned down to one. If the fourth is 12, the pattern is the same.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.r.a: Earlier you made several different patterns.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.o.b: It is not pinned down to one, but the fifth numbers are all the same.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.r.b: Find the number after 6, 8, 10, 12 and the number after 3, 6, 9, 12 and compare them.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.o.c: It is not pinned down to one. There are patterns with a different fifth number.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.r.c: You thought about the fact that the amount it grows by is different for each pattern, so the next number is different.
x-m-e1-10.s.s2.explain: After 6, 8, 10, 12 comes 14, after 3, 6, 9, 12 comes 15, and after 9, 10, 11, 12 comes 13. Even if the fourth number is the same, if the pattern is different, the fifth number is different.
x-m-e1-10.s.s3.prompt: Write the fifth number of each of the two patterns you made, and say how the two patterns are different.
x-m-e1-10.s.s3.hint.0: Find the number that comes after the fourth number in my pattern.
x-m-e1-10.s.s3.hint.1: Compare how much the amount it grows by is in the two patterns.
x-m-e1-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check again that the fifth number you wrote fits the pattern?
x-m-e1-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you clearly write in what way the two patterns are different (the amount it grows by)?
x-m-e1-10.s.s3.model.0: After 6, 8, 10, 12 comes 14, and after 3, 6, 9, 12 comes 15. The amount it grows by is different, 2 and 3, so the fifth number is different.
x-m-e1-10.s.s3.model.1: The first pattern grows by 2, so it becomes 14, and the second grows by 3, so it becomes 15. So the fifth numbers are different from each other.
